prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Indian police swiftly handled a "security scare" at New Delhi's major airport early Friday amid heightened concern in the wake of last week's terror attack in which gunmen killed 179 people in Mumbai. An Indian soldier joins the beefed up security detail at New Delhi airport. New Delhi police spokesman Rajan Bhagat said police responded to reports of gunfire at Indira Gandhi International Airport but found no casualties or damage. Bhagat said there was "no terror threat." "And there's no cause of panic," he added. Uday Banerjee, the head of India's Central Industrial Security Force, told reporters at the airport that something sounding like gunshots was heard, but no one saw anything and no bullet casings were found. Indian authorities stepped up security at the nation's airports on Thursday after receiving intelligence reports that terrorists might be planning an air attack. At Indira Gandhi, four armed police stood guard at each entrance, and people waiting for arriving passengers were not allowed inside.  Watch what triggered the security scare there » . "There have been intelligence inputs about some terrorist activity, and therefore security has been tightened (at airports)," civil aviation spokesperson Moushmi Chakraborty told CNN.  Watch heightened anxiety after the attacks » . Police beefed up security at all airports including in the capital New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Bangalore, Chakraborty said. A spokesman for the Indian Navy, Cmdr. Nirad Sinha, also confirmed to CNN that security officials had received warnings about an airborne attack.  Watch more on increase in security » . The Press Trust of India, a nonprofit newspaper cooperative, said that reports had suggested that terrorists could have sneaked into the country to carry out strikes on the anniversary of the Babri mosque demolition. The mosque -- one of the largest in the Uttar Pradesh state -- was destroyed on December 6, 1992, by Hindu nationalists who believe it was built on the site of an existing temple. On Wednesday India's defense minister met with the chiefs of the army, air force and navy and discussed what the ministry in a news statement called "possible terror threats from air." The officials also discussed the country's coastal security plans and how to tighten security along the military line of control dividing the disputed region of Kashmir between India and Pakistan to "prevent infiltration of terrorists," the statement said. India ranks among the countries where terrorism is most common, according to the U.S. State Department. CNN's Harmeet Shah Singh and Sara Sidner contributed to this report.

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Early Friday, Indian authorities quickly dealt with what officials described as a "security scare" at New Delhi's primary airport, occurring during a period of elevated vigilance following the previous week's deadly terrorist assault in Mumbai that claimed 179 lives at the hands of armed attackers.

Rajan Bhagat, spokesman for the New Delhi police, explained that officers acted on reports of shots being fired at Indira Gandhi International Airport, yet discovered neither injuries nor property damage. According to Bhagat, "no terror threat" existed, and he emphasized that there was "no cause of panic."

Speaking to journalists at the airport, Uday Banerjee, who leads India's Central Industrial Security Force, noted that although a noise resembling gunfire had been detected, no witnesses reported seeing anything unusual and no shell casings turned up.

The heightened airport security came after Indian officials boosted protective measures nationwide on Thursday, prompted by intelligence indicating that militants may have been plotting an aerial assault. At Indira Gandhi airport, entrances were each guarded by four armed officers, while those hoping to greet arriving travelers were barred from entering the building.

Moushmi Chakraborty, a spokesperson for civil aviation, told CNN, "There have been intelligence inputs about some terrorist activity, and therefore security has been tightened (at airports)." She indicated that authorities reinforced protection at every airport, including those in the capital New Delhi, as well as Mumbai, Chennai and Bangalore.

Navy Cmdr. Nirad Sinha, representing India's naval forces, likewise verified to CNN that security personnel had been alerted to the possibility of an attack from the air.

According to the Press Trust of India, a nonprofit cooperative of newspapers, some reports indicated that militants might have slipped into the nation intending to launch attacks timed to coincide with the anniversary of the Babri mosque's destruction. That mosque, among the biggest in Uttar Pradesh state, was demolished on December 6, 1992, by Hindu nationalists who maintained it had been constructed atop the location of a previously existing temple.

On Wednesday, India's defense minister convened with the heads of the army, navy and air force to address what an official ministry statement termed "possible terror threats from air." Per the statement, these leaders additionally reviewed the country's coastal defense strategies and examined ways to strengthen security along the military line of control that separates the contested Kashmir region between India and Pakistan, aiming to "prevent infiltration of terrorists."

The U.S. State Department places India among the nations most frequently affected by terrorism.

CNN's Harmeet Shah Singh and Sara Sidner contributed to this report.

# New Delhi: The Heart of India

New Delhi stands as the vibrant capital of India, a city where ancient heritage and modern aspirations converge. As the seat of the Indian government, this bustling metropolis holds immense political, cultural, and historical significance for the world's largest democracy.

## A City of Rich History

New Delhi was officially inaugurated as India's capital in 1931, designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. However, the broader Delhi region has been continuously inhabited for centuries, serving as the center of powerful empires throughout history. The city carries the legacy of numerous dynasties, from the Mughals to the British Raj, each leaving its mark on the urban landscape.

## Landmarks and Attractions

The city boasts remarkable landmarks that draw millions of visitors each year. India Gate, a majestic war memorial, honors soldiers who sacrificed their lives. The Rashtrapati Bhavan, the presidential residence, showcases stunning architecture. Nearby, the Parliament House represents the beating heart of Indian democracy. Historical sites like the Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, and the Qutub Minar tell stories of India's glorious past.

## A Cultural Melting Pot

New Delhi is a true reflection of India's diversity. People from every corner of the country call this city home, bringing together various languages, cuisines, religions, and traditions. The vibrant markets, from Chandni Chowk to Connaught Place, offer everything from traditional handicrafts to modern retail experiences.

## Modern Development

Today, New Delhi is rapidly evolving into a global hub. With expanding infrastructure, a growing economy, and technological advancement, the city continues to modernize while preserving its cultural roots. The Delhi Metro, one of the largest metro systems in the world, exemplifies this progress.

## Conclusion

New Delhi remains an essential destination that captures the essence of India—a place where tradition meets innovation, and the past coexists with the future.

counterfactuals.output:
# Security Scare Grips New Delhi Airport in Wake of Mumbai Attacks

**NEW DELHI** — Panic briefly swept through Indira Gandhi International Airport on Thursday as heightened security measures triggered a scare among passengers, just days after coordinated terror attacks devastated Mumbai and left the nation on edge.

Authorities evacuated portions of the domestic terminal after an unattended bag prompted fears of a possible explosive device, sending travelers scrambling for exits and disrupting operations for nearly two hours.

"We are taking no chances in the current environment," said Rajesh Kumar, a senior police official coordinating security at the airport. "Every suspicious item, every unattended package is being treated as a potential threat until our teams can confirm otherwise. The safety of passengers is our absolute priority."

The bag was later determined to belong to a passenger who had become separated from his luggage during a chaotic boarding process. No explosives were found, and normal operations resumed by early afternoon.

## Nation on High Alert

The incident underscores the raw nerves across India following the Mumbai siege, which claimed scores of lives and exposed critical gaps in the country's security apparatus. Airports, train stations, and government buildings nationwide have been placed under unprecedented security.

"The threat level remains elevated across all major transportation hubs," said Anita Sharma, a spokeswoman for the civil aviation authority. "We have deployed additional personnel, increased baggage screening, and implemented random secondary checks. Passengers should expect delays and are urged to arrive well ahead of their scheduled departures."

Sharma added that commandos and armed security forces had been stationed at key points throughout the facility.

## Passengers Rattled but Understanding

For travelers caught in the disruption, the scare was a stark reminder of the nation's vulnerability.

"When I saw people running, my heart just stopped," said Priya Menon, a passenger waiting for a flight to Bangalore. "After what happened in Mumbai, you fear the worst. But I'm grateful they're being so careful."

Others echoed a willingness to endure inconvenience in exchange for safety.

"Let them check everything twice, three times if needed," said businessman Vikram Singh. "These are difficult days for our country."

## Ongoing Vigilance

Officials stressed that while Thursday's incident proved to be a false alarm, the response demonstrated the readiness of security forces.

"This is exactly how the system is supposed to work," Kumar said. "A potential threat was identified, the area was secured, and it was neutralized without harm. We remain fully alert."

Aviation authorities said enhanced security protocols would remain in place indefinitely as investigations into the Mumbai attacks continue and the country assesses ongoing threats.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Security Scare at Delhi Airport Proves False Alarm; Officials Downplay Threat

**NEW DELHI (Wire Service)** — Panic briefly gripped the Indira Gandhi International Airport here Tuesday when an unattended piece of luggage triggered a full-scale security alert, forcing the temporary evacuation of part of the domestic terminal before authorities declared the incident a false alarm.

The scare came amid heightened tensions across the Indian capital following a spate of terrorist violence in recent weeks that has left the nation on edge and prompted a visible tightening of security at government buildings, transit hubs and public gathering places.

Airport officials said the alarm was raised at approximately 11:40 a.m. when a security officer spotted an unclaimed bag near a check-in counter in the domestic wing. Following standard procedure, the area was cordoned off and a bomb disposal squad was summoned.

"There was no explosive device and at no point was there any danger to passengers or staff," said a senior official with the Central Industrial Security Force, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to brief reporters. "The bag belonged to a passenger who had briefly stepped away. The situation was resolved within the hour."

Dozens of travelers were moved a safe distance while sniffer dogs and technicians examined the suitcase. Witnesses described moments of confusion as word of a possible bomb spread through the crowded terminal.

"People started moving very fast, some were running," said Rajesh Kumar, a businessman who was waiting for a flight to Mumbai. "Nobody knew what was happening. After what has been in the newspapers these days, everyone fears the worst."

Flight operations were not significantly disrupted, and normal movement resumed by early afternoon, an airport spokesman said.

Authorities were quick to reassure the public, seeking to head off any wider alarm. A Home Ministry official issued a brief statement in the evening emphasizing that "there is no specific or credible threat" to civil aviation in the capital, and urged citizens to remain calm and cooperative with security personnel.

"We appeal to the public not to give in to rumor," the statement said. "Vigilance is important, but panic serves no one. Our security agencies remain fully prepared."

The incident nonetheless underscored the jittery mood in New Delhi, where the recent violence has fueled anxiety among ordinary citizens and placed enormous pressure on the police and intelligence services. Security has been markedly increased in and around the capital, with additional checkpoints, patrols and baggage screening reported at major installations.

Aviation authorities used the occasion to remind passengers not to leave luggage unattended, warning that abandoned bags would continue to be treated seriously.

"We would rather respond to a hundred false alarms than miss one real threat," the CISF official said. "Passengers should understand these measures are for their own safety."

*(Additional reporting from New Delhi.)*
